subject: nineTailedKitsune
pitch:
Category: Fantastical creature.
Subject: nine-tailed kitsune fox with spirit flames.
Style: high-fantasy anime.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a single TypeScript module for a stylized nine-tailed kitsune fox with spirit flames, thinking through proportions like a 0.7m shoulder height and sketching the skeleton hierarchy starting from the root bone.

I'm mapping out the spine, neck, and head joint chains, then designing nine tail chains fanning from the hips, with tail tips carrying flame-card textures and orbiting kitsunebi orbs for the spirit fire effect, aiming for a white-and-crimson color scheme with gold accents while being careful to use the builder API correctly.

Still defining the spine chain...

Now I'm adding the neck as a chain of two joints curving upward from the spine's end, then attaching the head joint with a forward-and-slightly-upward direction so I can later reference local directions like forward/up/right for positioning facial features.

Adding jaw joint using head's local direction helper...

I'm thinking through how to shape the skull: rather than risky scale options on parts, I'll scale the sphere geometry directly along model axes (width, height, length) before passing it in, keeping orientation aligned with world axes. For the snout, I'm considering a frustum or cone shape built with a sweep.

Planning the blocky puppet-style muzzle using frustumBox for the upper snout and lower jaw, attached to the jaw bone, with a small dark sphere as the nose tip, and anime-style eyes added as decals on the head.

I realize using `b.surface(skull).around(skull.at).at(azimuth, elevation)` gives a more accurate hit point on the curved surface than guessing coordinates manually. I'll define the eye position using azimuth (mirrored per side) and a fixed elevation, then decal the texture at that computed hit point with an appropriate size.

Setting mirror to s<0, then working through the fox ear geometry: extruding a triangular outline at the head with thickness for a flat plane facing forward, and tilting it outward based on side.

For coloring I'm thinking cream outside, crimson inside, keeping tip styling simple. Now moving on to planning the four legs with a limb system.

With 4 points per leg chain that's 3 spans needing bend directions and names like hipL/kneeL/hockL/pawL, with the leg root positioned relative to the spine and side determined by sign of x. I'm defining the sweep radius profile tapering from hip to paw, something like [0.06, 0.045, 0.03...].

For coloring I want white legs with darker "sock" gradients toward the paws, kitsune-style, using a gradient function between fur color and a darker sock tone positioned along the leg. Then I'm adding a paw shape as a flattened sphere geometry positioned at the tip joint so the foot sits near ground level.

I'm skipping toe details for simplicity, and adding bulkier thigh geometry for the hind legs using a tapered sweep radius profile. For the body, I'm planning a sweep/loft along a catmull-rom path running from the rump through the spine to the chest.

I'm figuring out root joint placement so the hips serve as the origin with no parent, and adjusting the spine chain start position to align cleanly with the body sweep path rather than overlapping awkwardly.

For the body shape itself, I'm planning a sweep along the spine chain using a radius function that widens toward the chest, giving deeper and taller ellipse cross-sections there, with legs and tail parented appropriately to spine or hip joints, and the neck handled as its own separate sweep.

I'm working out the parametrization for the combined spine-neck path, estimating segment lengths so the chest radius bump lands around t≈0.7, and sketching a radius function that tapers from wider hips to narrower neck across that t range.

Now I'm building a piecewise-linear interpolation helper for the radius keyframes, then planning fur cards for a white neck ruff scattered onto the surface, plus thinking through how to add crimson stripe markings onto the body.

I think using sectors is simpler and safer here, giving a narrow red dorsal stripe without complex angle math. For kumadori-style leg markings, I'll add gradient paint transitioning from fur color to a darker sock-like tone, maybe with a subtle red/gold ring near the base of each leg.

Now for the nine tails fanned out from the rump: I'm planning each tail's root position and spreading them across roughly -80° to +80° in azimuth, with the central tails sitting slightly higher than the outer ones for a natural fan shape.

Each tail tip curls upward like flame, tapering from a fluffy mid-plume down to a fine point using a radius sweep. I'm spacing all nine tails across a ±70° rear arc in three vertical layers so they fan out without overlapping, defining direction vectors per tail index.

Still working out tail geometry...

I'm widening the tip lateral spread for a fuller fan shape, keeping center tails taller and outer ones curling outward like a classic peacock-fan kitsune tail. Now I'm working out naming conventions for the tail joint chains, making sure each tail's joints get unique, regex-valid names tied to the hip parent.

I'll switch to letter-based chain names like "tailA", "tailB" with joints "tailA1" etc. to avoid ambiguous numbering, and I'm checking the total joint budget stays under the 160 limit across tails, legs, spine, and neck. For coloring, I'm thinking white fur fading to crimson toward the mid and tip, with a spirit-flame effect glowing at the very ends.

Defining gradient paint for tail coloring...

I should compute flow direction as the tail's tangent at each point along the path, using the closest parameter on the curve. For the tuft texture itself, I'll use a simple pointed leaf shape in an SVG, tinted via the color parameter rather than drawn with its own colors.

For the spirit flame effect at the tail tips, I'm thinking of using cross-oriented cards with a flame-shaped SVG texture, cyan tinted, drawn in actual color (outer blue, inner cyan-white) using gradients rather than relying on tinting.

Since cards are shaded as regular surfaces with standard material, they won't glow naturally, but I could try grabbing the returned meshes afterward and tweaking their material's emissive property to fake a glow.

Actually that risks getting lost during mesh merging or texture atlas baking, so I'll skip it. For the floating foxfire orbs, I'm planning a ring of 5 small icosahedron spheres around the fox at varying heights, each topped with a flame card cross, positioned independently of any bone since they're meant to hover rather than attach to the body.

I'm also considering small spirit-fire flames at each paw, cheap blue cards sitting near the floor frames to give the fox's feet a glowing aura. For the face, I'm planning eyes as SVG decals with an anime style: big almond shapes, dark upper lash lines, and a gold iris with a slit pupil for that foxy look.

I'm working out the eye geometry and eyeliner direction so the mirrored decal doesn't flip the upswept outer corner the wrong way between the left and right eyes.

Writing SVG code...

Adjusting iris sizing to fit within the eye shape, then layering a darker eyelid path on top to cover the upper edge so the eyes read naturally without needing pixel-perfect precision.

I also need to add the red kumadori marking—a tapered crimson stripe sweeping outward from the eye's outer corner. I'm considering widening the viewBox so this decal has room to extend past the eye itself, accounting for mirroring between left and right sides.

Working through the skull geometry, I'm placing the eye decal at roughly ±38° azimuth and 10° elevation on the 0.1-radius sphere, computing the resulting x/z offsets so the flat decal wraps correctly, and adding a guard against a null hit when targeting the skull part. Then I move to the nose, planning a dark sphere at the snout tip, with the snout itself built as a frustum tapering from the head's forward-facing surface down to a smaller tip.

Now I'm figuring out the lower jaw geometry, defining it as a frustum box anchored to the jaw bone with joint and aim points derived from the head's local coordinates, and sizing it down from the wider jaw base to a narrower front edge.

Good, the gap between jaw and upper muzzle closes nicely now. I also want spiky cheek ruffs on the sides — pointed anime-style fur tufts extruded outward from the face, so I'm sketching an outline in the frontal plane with sharp alternating points, being careful the shape doesn't self-intersect.

Checking the path doesn't self-intersect, I confirm the segments stay properly ordered without crossing, then I move to positioning the shape using local coordinates with thickness along the cross-product axis.

For the cheek tufts, I'm pinning them near the skull's side at roughly ±85° azimuth, close to the skull radius so they sit just under the surface with a bit of thickness. For the ears, I'm placing them toward the back-top of the head and thinking through how to tilt the ear outline outward using a skewed y-axis so the ears angle away from the skull rather than standing straight up.

Checking that the perpendicular axes stay orthogonal for the mirrored ear works out fine since the dot product cancels. Now I'm defining the ear outline points with a sharp tip and smoothed base corners, setting thickness and bevel values, then starting on the smaller crimson inner-ear shape.

Still writing geometry...

Now I'm thinking about positioning the ears relative to the skull sphere, and considering adding a forehead decal, maybe a crescent or kumadori-style mark in red or gold.

For accessories, I'm considering a gold tasseled collar or beaded necklace—computing a neck loop from the joint, sweeping a rope around it, and spacing beads or bells along that loop.

Then I'm thinking about a crescent-shaped forehead ornament, perhaps a thin gold torus arc placed at the forehead using a stick orientation, though I need to check how the torus plane aligns with the surface normal there.

This torus crescent orientation is getting too fiddly to nail down precisely, so I'll simplify by using an octahedron as a small gold gem for the forehead instead, paired with a red diamond decal marking. I'll skip the ofuda idea and consider adding a gold shide element plus red markings elsewhere like the tails.

For the limbs, I'm painting banded regions along the leg height to create sock, anklet, and fur zones, and considering red kumadori-style markings on the upper limbs and shoulders. For the body I'm thinking about a custom paint function using noise to create a mottled crimson swirl pattern over white fur.

Simplifying toward a more distinctive look, I'm considering crimson sectors or flame-shaped markings on the flanks with a golden underbelly, trying out a simple reddish hex color for the patches rather than a complex procedural swirl.

Writing swirl decal paths...

Now I'm defining the fur colors with a cream-white base and a cooler shade for shading, then checking leg attachment points and lengths to make sure the foreleg geometry bends naturally from shoulder to foot.

For the hind legs, I'm setting them up as digitigrade with knee forward and hock back, adjusting the longer segment lengths so there's more bend to achieve a natural standing pose, with the paw positioned slightly forward for visual balance.

I'm sizing and positioning a small scaled sphere for the paw just ahead of the foot joint, then resolving which joint to treat as the leg's tip for the sweep operation, falling back to the last joint in the chain if no explicit tip exists. Then I'm defining the radius values that taper along the leg sweep from thicker near the hip to thinner near the paw.

I'm working through the vertical math to make sure the rounded end cap of the leg sweep and the paw sphere both come close enough to the floor to read as ground contact, accepting a couple millimeters of gap as within tolerance relative to overall model height.

Then I'm adding simple sphere bulges at the hip and shoulder joints, scaled to be slightly flattened, to suggest thigh and shoulder muscle mass without adding extra toe or claw detail.

For the tail, I'm planning a small fur tuft at the rump base, then building the tail as a chain of bones following a smooth curve computed from a Catmull-Rom path, parented to the hips. I'll sweep that chain with a tapering radius profile that shrinks to zero at the tip with pointed caps, and I'm noting that if there are multiple tails, their overlapping bases near the rump won't be visually problematic since they're hidden by the body geometry.

Now I'm adding small curvature variations so each tail has its own wave and a slight outward curl at the tip. At each tail's tip point I'm placing a flame card using a frame oriented upward, sized around 0.2 by 0.34, alternating between blue and purple flame textures across the different tails.

Actually using chain.at(1) directly is cleaner since it already carries the bone and tangent, letting flames naturally continue along the tail's upward direction without manually specifying bones. I'll add a few smaller secondary flames further down the tail at chain.at(0.85), leaned along the tangent for variety.

Writing SVG flame paths...

I'm deciding to skip the paw flames since they'd overlap awkwardly, and instead go with a ring of floating flame orbs around the fox—settling on 7 orbs and sketching rough positions at varying radii and heights, making sure they stay clear of the tail fan area.

Placing orbs...

I'll skip adding a role since nothing fits, and construct each orb as a small icosahedron geometry positioned at the joint. I'm deciding to skip adding a stone dais or base since the model should stand directly at y=0, keeping the composition simple without extra ground props.

Instead I'll add a thin magic-circle decal on the ground, using a flat circle geometry just above y=0 textured with an SVG-based pale cyan pattern, visible from above and parented to the hips so it reads as grounded fox-fire without dipping below the floor.

Adding inner ring at 60, checking alpha cutoff for transparency, and sizing the tail fan and orb radius within the circle's footprint. I'm also confirming orientation axes and material shading before moving to the tuft texture SVG, sketching a pointed leaf shape for the ruff card.

I'm shaping the tuft texture so it's wide at the base and tapers to a point at the top, filled white so it can be tinted by whatever color is applied, and planning to reuse it for tail fluff, neck ruff, and chest. Then I'm scattering these cards across the tail sweep surface using a minimum-distance scatter function to place them, aiming for roughly 22 cards per tail across many tails.

For the flow direction, each card leans toward the tail tip by computing the tangent along the tail path at the closest point, tinting each card with the paint color sampled at its root so the gradient carries through naturally. I'm keeping bend at 0 to avoid extra geometry overhead.

Now I'm setting up the head and neck ruff cards, scattering them along a restricted band of the body sweep (filtering by position and normal to target the upper-back region), with cards leaning backward and downward, moderate size, fur-colored, around 60 cards with a minimum spacing of 0.04.

For the chest, I'm adding forward-facing tufts filtered by position and outward-facing normals, merging them into the same scatter group since the triangle budget stays comfortable overall.

For body surface detail, I'm defining color sectors on the body sweep — a dorsal stripe constrained to a limited length range so it doesn't bleed into the neck, plus a subtler cream belly band — while leaving the rest of the surface as the base fur color.

Now I'm working out flank swirl decals, placing them on the body sweep around a point near the shoulder and mirroring the azimuth angle for left versus right sides so the pattern faces outward correctly on each flank, with the decal's facing direction flipped depending on which side is being viewed from.

I'm placing the forehead gem as a small gold octahedron stuck at the same hit point as a red diamond decal, then considering whether to add facial streaks, a mouth line, or whiskers — deciding to skip most of these and keep just the eyes, nose, and maybe an eyebrow.

Now I'm working out a gold neck collar: tracing a loop around the neck joint, sweeping a red rope along it, then distributing small gold icosahedron beads along that loop using the frame from each point to orient them correctly.

For the bell, I'm locating a point near the front-underside of the neck via a nearest-surface hit, placing a small gold sphere there with a tassel rather than trying to derive "front" from the loop's angle convention, which felt too ambiguous. Skipping earrings and tail bells, and now I'm troubleshooting a case where the neck joint placement causes the loop's cutting plane to miss the body surface entirely.

I'm settling on 4 spine points giving 3 spans and joints (spine1-3), with hind legs parented to spine1 and forelegs to spine3, placing the shoulder around z=0.28. I'm working out the actual spine point coordinates along the back, considering whether 5 points would give finer control.

Now I'm laying out neck points as two spans (neck1, neck2), parenting the neck to the last spine joint, and placing the head joint at the neck's end, then concatenating the spine and neck paths together.

Rather than build each chain's curve separately and risk a tangent discontinuity at the seam, I'm reconsidering: build one single catmull curve across all body and neck points, then slice it per chain using the t-values found via closestT for each joint location, so spine and neck segments share a smooth continuous curve.

Now I'm moving on to placing the head: figuring out the skull center position relative to the neck's endpoint, estimating its radius and non-uniform scale, and setting a roughly horizontal facing direction.

Checking overall proportions - shoulder height, head height with ears, total height with tail and flame effects - to confirm the fox silhouette reads as a tall alert kitsune.

Now I'm setting up the decal system, applying a texture generated from SVG markup onto the skull surface. Writing SVG code for the eyes...

Adding a darker orange lower iris, a slit pupil, and two white highlight dots for glint, then drawing a thick upper eyelid that overlaps the top of the iris for a heavy-lidded look.

Checking that the iris stays within the white boundary of the eye and doesn't clip past the outline — it looks fine. I'm also tallying the overall flat color palette (fur tones, red, gold, dark, socks, nose, orb colors) to stay within a reasonable limit, and now setting up a gradient fill for the tail.

Building the leg paint logic...

Defining body radii keyframes...

Still writing leg geometry...

Setting radius tapers for front and hind leg sweeps, then adding a scaled sphere for the paw geometry with a dark sock color, skipping tiny toe details for simplicity.

Confirming that scaling a geometry returns the geometry itself, then placing the hind paw at the correct negative z-offset from its foot target. I'm adding shoulder and hip bulge spheres with specific scale ratios positioned at the leg and thigh joints, colored to match the fur.

Now I'm setting up a fluffy tail tuft at the rump, then moving into head construction — defining the head joint parented to the neck chain's last joint, following the established parenting pattern (spine parented to hips, neck to spine, legs to the first spine joint). I'm starting the skull geometry as a scaled sphere attached to the head joint.

Still working on the muzzle and nose, placing a frustum-shaped snout and a small dark nose sphere relative to the head joint's local coordinates.

Now I'm adding the jaw bone and its box shape, positioning the lower jaw joint and aligning the gap between the upper muzzle and lower jaw boxes so they meet cleanly.

Skipping that seam detail for now. I'm considering cheek tufts, ears, eyes, forehead, and a small blue kitsune-bi flame crest between the ears at the top of the skull, sized to sit nicely without covering the face.

Then I'm thinking through neck ruff scatter, the orb section with its magic circle, and rig ordering—joints and chains need to come before geometry is built. For pose, I'll keep it neutral rather than opening the jaw.

Writing tail segment loop...

I'm checking the tail proportions—total length around 1.3m against a 0.7m fox body feels right for a dramatic nine-tail fan, and I'm shaping the tip radius with a smooth taper curve while checking that adjacent tails don't collide at their base spacing.

Since the fan currently reads as flat like a peacock from the side, I'm adding depth variation by alternating back offsets between tails so the fur has more volume, then plan to use the end of each tail chain as the base position for flame elements, moving next into building the actual fur card geometry.

Adding flame cards at the tail tip and side flares, orienting them along the tangent frames so they stand correctly off the swept tail surface.

For the fox details, I'm checking the decal call defaults for direction and up vectors, and placing eye hits using the surface sampling method anchored to the skull frame's position.

Then I'm working out the pupil placement math: since the pupil sits off-center in the texture, I need to shift the azimuth angle for each eye to account for that offset, and verifying the resulting eye separation looks right relative to the head width.

Checking the snout overlap: tracing forward from the skull center, I'm computing whether the snout's tapering width at the eye's forward position would actually occlude part of the decal, since the snout geometry narrows as it extends forward and the pupil span might partially fall within that narrower region.

Checking the eye and pupil positions against the snout's taper more precisely, I'm finding the eye's inner edge still overlaps the snout boundary at that depth, since the snout half-width there is close to the skull radius itself—meaning the snout barely protrudes past the skull at that point, so the eyes remain partially masked.

That should be fine, I'm confirming the snout sits inside the skull front correctly, and now checking ear placement sits properly on the skull's top curvature and the cheek tuft position relative to the skull side.

For the cheek tufts, I'm thinking they should extrude outward sideways with a slight backward tilt so they read as fluff from the front but stay thin from the side, handling the orientation vectors by hand rather than relying on normalization. Now I'm moving on to the orbs and then setting up a collar loop anchored at the neck's first joint.

I'm reconsidering which neck joint to anchor the collar at — joint[1] sits at the mid-neck where the bone's direction gives a good cutting plane through the body tube at the right radius. I also want to make sure the ruff cards (angled outward fluff) visually cover the collar rope rather than clash with it, so I'm tuning the ruff's z-range and the rope's lift and radius so they overlap cleanly.

Then I'm figuring out the bell placement — casting a ray from a point near the front underside of the neck outward to find where it exits the body surface, so the bell sits naturally where the neck meets the chest, just below where the head will eventually attach.

Now I'm writing the helper for generating a 9-pointed star polygon by computing vertex angles and connecting every fourth point around the circle, for the ground circle SVG pattern.

Also planning the concentric rings with varying stroke widths, scaled for a 512px canvas, plus small vertex circles and a ring of tick marks between radii 78 and 84, checking that stroke widths stay visible at the final scale factor.

I'm settling on final color choices—cyan accents with a gold inner ring—and deciding on texture size (512) considering atlas budget constraints. Then I shift to placing the magic circle itself as a ground-facing disc attached to the hips bone, oriented so its front face points upward.

Now I'm also thinking through TypeScript correctness: making sure point arrays are properly typed as 3-length tuples for the catmull curve input, and considering how callback parameters should be typed rather than left as "any" to satisfy strict type checking.

I'm also being careful about unused variables causing errors, and double-checking how the rng function is passed around and used — whether it's a seed-returning generator or called directly to produce random values for scattering.

Now I'm defining my color palette: warm cream and fur tones, deep reds and a rose-colored tail tip, golds, dark purples for sock and shadow details, plus a nose, eye, and bead color.

Setting up leg paint zones with sock color at the base, a thin gold ring, then fur above, with a subtle red tint for front legs. I'm starting the builder structure, defining the hips joint as the root with a spine role before building out the rest of the skeleton.

Building the body curve path through a series of control points, then splitting it into a spine chain and a neck chain at the point closest to the shoulder, making sure the subdivision still preserves enough detail along each segment.

Setting joint counts and resampling by arc length so joints land at even spacing, placing the head joint at the path's endpoint with its orientation vector, and confirming the leg chains attach to the correct spine joint index before sweeping the body mesh along the spine and neck bones.

Writing a helper function that interpolates between keyframe pairs linearly, finding the bracketing keys for a given time value and blending the two associated numbers proportionally. I'm noting that linear interpolation produces visible kinks in the radius profile, so a smoothed interpolation would look better even at low polygon counts.

Now I'm applying skull surface decals, generating flame and tuft SVG assets with layered colors, and scattering ruff tufts across the body surface using filtered sample points based on height and normal direction, then placing fur-colored cards with randomized size, lean, and bend at those scatter locations.

Adding eye decals...

Still writing orb loop...

I'm double-checking the ground circle positioning and rig names, then making sure color constants like CREAM, RED, SOCK, and GOLD are all actually used where intended for the ears, nose, and paws. I need to figure out how to type the cheek tuft outline array, possibly declaring it inline rather than importing an uncertain type.

I'll just inline the literal tuples directly in each function call instead of fighting with the type alias, since they're contextually typed that way anyway — simpler for ears, cheeks, and ear tips alike. Now I'm working out the ear's local coordinate directions, making sure the up/side/thickness vectors stay perpendicular, and positioning the ear base relative to the head joint.

Still writing extrude calls...

Setting the eye sclera color, then checking that the extrude function correctly handles local vertex positions, and placing a flame crest between the ears. I'm verifying the model faces forward and stays centered, confirming the front legs attach to the right spine joint, and setting up the tail chain with a catmull-rom curve and tapered sweep radii.

Defining the tail paint gradient from fur color to red tip, then setting up the leg paint function signature. I'm double-checking the limb bend hints for the forelegs and hind legs so the knees and hocks bend in anatomically correct directions, then finalizing the hip joint position.
